questions.q: In an AR(1) model x_t = c + phi_1*x_(t-1) + eps_t, what does a coefficient with |phi_1| < 1 imply?
options: The series has a unit root and is non-stationary
Shocks decay over time and the series is stationary
The model is actually an MA(1) model in disguise
The series variance is undefined
questions.explain: When |phi_1| < 1, the influence of past shocks shrinks over time, which is the condition for the AR(1) process to be stationary. phi_1 = 1 would be the unit-root random walk case instead.

questions.q: What is the key structural difference between how AR and MA models propagate a shock?
options: AR effects cut off sharply after p lags; MA effects decay gradually forever
AR effects decay gradually and never fully vanish; MA effects cut off sharply after q lags
There is no difference — AR and MA are mathematically identical
MA models cannot be stationary under any parameter values
questions.explain: AR models propagate shocks through the autoregressive feedback loop, so influence fades gradually but technically never hits exactly zero. MA models only include shocks up to q periods back, so the effect disappears completely after that.

questions.q: Why would an analyst prefer an ARMA(1,1) model over a pure AR(10) model that fits similarly well?
options: ARMA models are always more accurate regardless of data
Pure AR models cannot be fit using statsmodels
ARMA(1,1) may capture similar dynamics with far fewer parameters, which is a parsimony advantage
AR models cannot include a constant term
questions.explain: A core motivation for ARMA is parsimony: combining a small AR and MA term can reproduce the fit of a much longer pure-AR or pure-MA model with fewer estimated parameters, which also tends to generalize better out of sample.

questions.q: What does the invertibility condition on an MA(q) model guarantee?
options: That the series has zero mean
That the MA roots lie outside the unit circle, giving a unique set of theta coefficients
That the series cannot be forecast
That the MA model is equivalent to an AR(0) model
questions.explain: Invertibility requires the MA characteristic polynomial's roots to lie outside the unit circle. This lets the MA process be rewritten as an equivalent infinite AR process and ensures estimation finds a unique set of coefficients.

questions.q: In statsmodels, how do you fit a plain ARMA(1,1) model on an already-stationary series called `returns`?
options: ARIMA(returns, order=(1, 1, 1))
ARIMA(returns, order=(1, 0, 1))
VAR(returns).fit(1)
arch_model(returns, vol='Garch', p=1, q=1)
questions.explain: statsmodels folds ARMA into the ARIMA class: setting d=0 means no differencing is applied, so ARIMA(returns, order=(1, 0, 1)) is exactly an ARMA(1,1) model fit on the series as given.
